sentences.text: Tanius possessed a flat, elongated head featuring large openings above the temples and a narrow cheekbone.
Gregory S. Paul once estimated this dinosaur to reach seven meters in length and weigh two metric tons.
The spinous processes on its vertebrae were remarkably tall, measuring 3.2 times the height of the vertebral body.
The top surface of the third metatarsal bone displays a distinct crescent moon profile.
H. C. T'an uncovered the remains in April 1923 at Ch'ing-kang-kou village, located ten kilometers southeast of Lai Yang in Shandong.
The holotype specimen, cataloged as PMU R.240, originates from the Jiangjunding Formation of the Wangshi Series.
Carl Wiman formally named and described the type species Tanius sinensis in 1929.
The genus name honors the Chinese paleontologist Tan Xichou, while the species name references China.
Although the original specimen was largely complete, only fragments could be salvaged during the excavation process.
The holotype consists of the rear portion of a flat, elongated skull.
This animal shared its environment with Pinacosaurus, Micropachycephalosaurus, intermediate sauropods, coelurosaurs, and cheloniids.
Multiple localities of dinosaur eggs have been identified within the same formation where Tanius fossils were found.
Hadrosaur carcasses, including those of Tanius, were trapped and displaced by a mudflow event before rapid burial occurred.
At least twenty individuals of hadrosaurs, including Tanius, of various ages have been uncovered at these sites.
Tanius is a genus of hadrosauroid dinosaur.
It is classified within the family Hadrosauridae.
Recent analyses place Tanius as a basal member of Hadrosauridae, while other studies suggest it is even more basal within the broader Hadrosauroidea.
Tanius lived in China during the Late Cretaceous period.
It lived approximately 72 million years ago during the Campanian stage in what is now Asia.
The fossil record for Tanius spans from the Coniacian to the Campanian, between 89.8 and 72.2 million years ago.
Tanius inhabited a fluvial to lacustrine environment within the Jiangjunding Formation.
The climate where Tanius lived was generally warm and humid, though it began to dry out after the Jiangjunding Formation.
A 2017 study by Zhang et al. determined that T. sinensis and T. chingkankouensis are valid species, while T. laiyangensis is likely invalid.
A 2019 study re-assessed Tanius laiyangensis as a member of the Asian saurolophine clade Kritosaurini.
